Justification: Highest top-5 accuracy (85.0%) of the base-size encoders at equal top-1; RoBERTa-large adds 2.9 pp but has 2.8x the parameters, 7.4x the training time and gives no reply gain
A detector trained on situation descriptions fell from 56.9% to 48.2% on the user messages it actually receives
99.7% of training first utterances fit (mean 46.5 tokens)
Inside the fine-tuning ranges recommended for BERT (2e-5 to 5e-5) and used for RoBERTa (1e-5 to 3e-5)
Evidence: Devlin et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2019)

Justification: Batch size recommended for BERT/RoBERTa fine-tuning; 8 per step fits in 8 GB
Evidence: Devlin et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2019); hardware limit

Value: Up to 4, early stopping (patience 1), best checkpoint by validation accuracy
Justification: BERT recommends 2-4 fine-tuning epochs; keeping the best validation checkpoint prevents over-fitting
RoBERTa's fine-tuning setting; without warm-up our RoBERTa-large run diverged to 5.0% accuracy
Weight decay as used for BERT; clipping at 1.0 is the Transformers default and keeps updates stable
Fits the 8 GB GPU and trains faster; fixed seed for reproducibility

Value: 256 tokens over the last 4 user turns
Justification: Four joined turns exceed the 128-token training length, so the limit is doubled for the agent while the classifier itself is unchanged
The base settings diverged; 1e-5 is the lowest value of RoBERTa's fine-tuning range and batch 4 fits in memory

Value: Final-layer attention from the [CLS] token, eager attention
Justification: RoBERTa classifies from [CLS]; the default sdpa attention returns no weights, so eager attention is required

Value: Top 40% of content tokens, floor 3 and ceiling 14, merged into at most 3 phrases
Justification: A fixed count returns almost the whole message for short inputs, which adds nothing because the generator already has the message; the floor and ceiling stop very short and very long messages producing a useless cue list, and the three-phrase cap keeps the prompt short
Attention concentrates on frequent function words, so without this the cues are stopwords rather than what the person said
Matches the detector's training length, and cues should point at the current message rather than turns the person has moved past
The true emotion is in the top-3 for 76.5% of messages against 50.3% for top-1, and most errors are neighbouring emotions

Value: Greedy, at most 10 new tokens, fall back to d1 top-1
Justification: A classification decision should be deterministic; 100% of stage-1 outputs named a valid candidate
Highest rule adherence in the bake-off with detector and prompt fixed (65.3% vs 57.7% Qwen2.5-1.5B, 22.0% Gemma-3-4B)
NF4 preserves 16-bit quality while cutting memory about fourfold; measured peak use 3.40 GB on the 8 GB GPU
The developer's default for Qwen2.5-Instruct; identical for every system so differences come from design, not decoding
Nucleus sampling avoids the repetitive, degenerate text of pure greedy or beam decoding; identical for every system
The prompt asks for under 100 words (about 130 tokens); the longest final reply is 119 tokens, so no reply is cut off

Value: Under 100 words in the prompt, scored at 120
Justification: Short replies reduce burden on a distressed user; the 20-word margin tolerates small overshoots

Deferred rather than chosen: it would likely reduce the 58.7% boilerplate rate, but regenerating every reply would have invalidated the AI-judge scores and the human-evaluation items already built on them
Sampling rather than greedy or beam search, which are known to produce repetitive text; one fixed seed makes every reported run reproducible
Context matters for emotion recognition in conversation; 4 turns was best or joint best in 3 of 4 long scenarios, 6 turns degraded 2
Evidence: Poria et al. (2019); our scenario tests

Justification: Support conversations are short; verbatim history avoids losing emotional detail through summarisation
A question in every reply turns a long conversation into an interrogation; turn 1 keeps the evaluated rules

Value: Qwen2.5-1.5B in fp16; Phi-4-mini and Qwen2.5-7B in 4-bit NF4
Justification: The same quantisation as the final system, so a comparison measures the design and not the numeric format; 1.5B fits in fp16 within the budget
Low ranks are sufficient to adapt attention weights; alpha = 2 x rank scales the update

Value: q, k, v, o attention projections
Justification: The weight matrices studied for adaptation in LoRA
LoRA's GPT-2 settings; QLoRA uses 2e-4 and dropout 0.1 for models up to 13B
Evidence: Hu et al. (2022); Dettmers et al. (2023)

Justification: Same warm-up rule as the detector; batch fits 8 GB; paged optimisers avoid memory spikes
Evidence: Liu et al. (2019); Dettmers et al. (2023)

Value: Up to 3, best epoch by validation loss, early stopping (patience 1)
Justification: Validation loss rose after epoch 1 (1.4607 to 1.4626), so epoch 1 was kept
The longest training pair is 177 tokens, so nothing is truncated
Using the end-of-turn token as padding masked it from the loss: the original run never learned to stop (99% of replies hit the token limit)
A small sentence encoder that runs beside the two models within the memory budget

Value: 2, from the same emotion where possible
Justification: Enough to show a pattern without crowding out the rules; the pool falls back to the same emotion without the question filter, then to the whole corpus, when too few examples exist

Value: Keyword check over 13 phrases ("sounds", "I hear you", "makes sense", "must be", ...)
Justification: A transparent check anyone can re-run and audit; its weakness, that a reply validating a feeling in other words is not counted, is reported rather than hidden

Value: Count of '?' in the reply equals 1
Justification: Counts the behaviour the rule actually asks for; more than one question is the interrogation failure mode the design exists to avoid

Value: 120 words when scoring, 100 words in the prompt
Justification: The prompt asks for less than the checker enforces, so a reply is not failed for a few words of overrun; both numbers are fixed for every system compared

Value: The reply is passed back through d1 and compared with the conversation's gold emotion
Justification: Tests what the reply expresses rather than its form, against a label the system never saw; the detector reads replies it was not trained on, which is reported as a limitation
Trained on human empathy ratings of conversation turns; r = 0.544 with human ratings
Evidence: Giorgi et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2024)

Value: System averages over 300 replies only, never a single reply
Justification: Agreement with the judges is strong across systems (rho = 0.74) but weak within one, so the score carries meaning in aggregate and not per reply
Removes sampling noise so the same reply always gets the same score

Value: 64 conversations: shortest and longest per emotion
Justification: Covers all 32 emotions and both short and long messages within the 50-requests-per-day limit
Different developers from our models avoid self-preference; a panel reduces single-judge bias
Evidence: Panickssery et al. (2024); Verga et al. (2024)

Value: 512 replies: 8 systems x 64 conversations, both judges scoring every one
Justification: Mixing judge sets across systems would make the scores incomparable

Value: 8 situations x 3 replies, each rated 1-5 on three dimensions, plus one preference question
Justification: Rating as well as choosing gives every system a score on every situation, so the size of a difference can be measured and not only its direction; 24 ratings keeps the form short enough to avoid rater fatigue
Fixed before any experiment and identical for every system, so all comparisons are paired
Paired tests matched to the data type; Wilcoxon does not assume normal differences
More than the 1,000 resamples recommended for percentile intervals, giving stable limits

Value: Holm correction; significant only if adjusted p < 0.05 and CI excludes zero
Justification: Controls the family-wise error rate with more power than Bonferroni

Value: 50 messages, 3 warm-up, one system per run
Justification: Warm-up removes first-call overhead; separate runs keep memory readings clean
